fetched_contents.text: The accuracy of panoramic radiography as a screening of bone mineral density in women: a systematic review Abstract Objectives: A systematic review and meta-analysis of diagnostic test accuracy studies was conducted to assess if the radiomorphometric indexes observed in panoramic radiographies could estimate reduced bone mineral density (BMD) similarly to standard technique the bone densitometry (dual energy X-ray absorptiometry) in females older than 30 years. Methods: A systematic search in four databases was conducted until January 2019. Two evaluators performed data extraction and evaluation of risk of bias independently, and agreement was achieved by consensus. Data were synthesized on a subgroup meta-analysis with a random effect model and the hierarchical summary receiver-operating characteristic curve was used to calculate pooled estimates of studies. Results: Thirty three studies were included and 12 different radiomorphometric indexes identified, including Mandibular Cortical Index (MCI). The final number of cases pooled for the analysis was 5266 females.The MCI for BMD loss (osteopenia) presented values of sensitivity 0.81 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.78–0.84] and specificity 0.48 (95% CI, 0.45–0.50), while for osteoporosis sensitivity 0.35 (95% CI, 0.30–0.40) and specificity 0.88 (95% CI, 0.86–0.90). The mandibular cortical width presented values of sensitivity 0.58 (95% CI, 0.40–0.73), specificity 0.73 (95% CI, 0.60–0.83) for osteopenia, while for osteoporosis sensitivity 0.57 (95% CI, 0.36–0.76) and specificity 0.83 (95% CI, 0.68–0.92). Due to the high sensitivity, MCI presented a potential value as a screening tool for initial BMD loss (osteopenia), once tests presenting high sensitivity are described as rarely missing subjects with the disease. To the other hand, MCI to osteoporosis and Mandibular Cortical Width for both conditions are not recommended because presented specificity higher than sensitivity. Conclusion: The MCI can be recommended as a feasible tool to screen initial BMD loss (osteopenia) in females above 30 years old using panoramic radiography exams. Although a preliminary diagnosis could impact the reduction of osteoporotic fractures risk, a systematical evaluation using DXA might be impracticable. Panoramic radiographs (PR) and associated risk factors of osteoporosis have been used to assess BMD decrease employing radiomorphometric indexes (RIs), especially in postmenopausal females.10–12 Noteworthy, PR is a routine exam to diagnosis several clinical conditions in dentistry, presenting low radiation doses and a considerable low cos.13 However, a lack of evidence still remains about the accuracy of these RIs in osteoporosis detection. fetched_contents.text: Radiomorphometric indices of the mandible as indicators of decreased bone mineral density and osteoporosis – meta-analysis and systematic review Abstract This review aims to evaluate the accuracy of various mandibular radiomorphometric indices in comparison with DEXA BMD measurements in the diagnosis of osteopenia and osteoporosis based on a meta-analysis of the sensitivity and specificity of the indices. PRISMA statement was followed. The materials for analysis were collected in August 2023 by searching three databases: PubMed Central, Web of Science, and Scopus. The selection of studies consisted of three selection stages, and 64 articles were finally obtained. Quality assessment was performed with the QUADAS-2 tool, and the general methodological quality of retrieved studies was low. Statistical analysis was performed based on 2 × 2 tables and estimated sensitivity and specificity were obtained using SROC curves. The most used indices were MCI, MCW and PMI. The best results in detecting reduced BMD obtained for MCW ≤ 3 mm, estimated sensitivity and specificity were 0.712 (95% CI, 0.477–0.870) and 0.804 (95% CI, 0.589–0.921), respectively. The most prone to the risk of bias is the MCI due to the examiner’s subjectivism. Radiomorphometric indices of the mandible can be useful as a screening tool to identify patients with low BMD, but should not be used as a diagnostic method. Further research needs to focus on analysing the ability of the indices to detect osteoporosis and also in combination the indices with clinical parameters. Supplementary information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s00198-023-06949-7. Keywords: Bone mineral density, Dental radiography, Mandibular radiomorphometric indices, Metabolic bone disease, Panoramic radiography Introduction The decrease of bone mineral density (BMD) is caused by a change in the bone microstructure. This is due to several factors, including calcium deficiency, vitamin D deficiency, lack of physical activity and genetic factors. Common diseases associated with lowering BMD are osteopenia and osteoporosis. Significant BMD impairment in the course of osteoporosis leads to fractures. Osteoporotic fractures lead to a significant reduction in the quality of life, increasing morbidity, mortality, and disability [1]. The standard method used to measure bone mineral density is dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA). The differences between the reference BMD values and the measurements are expressed in standard deviations (SD) scores and defined as T-scores or Z-scores. The reference given by WHO is data on Caucasian women aged 20–29 years. The T-score describes the value of SD by which BMD differs from the mean expected in young healthy subjects, while the Z-score describes the value of SD by which BMD differs from the mean expected value for age and gender. A T-score between -1.0 and -2.5 SD represents osteopenia, which is usually a pre-osteoporosis condition. Osteoporosis is diagnosed when the T-score is equal to or lower than -2.5 SD [2]. In addition to the DEXA method, imaging techniques such as computed tomography (CT), qualitative ultrasound (QUS), and the technique of single or double photon absorptiometry (SPA or DPA) are also used for the diagnosis of osteoporosis [3]. Studies analysing the usefulness of radiomorphometric indicators of the mandible observed in pantomographic images in the screening or preliminary diagnosis of osteopenia and osteoporosis are becoming more and more popular. Although some research results indicate no relationship between these indicators and BMD measured with DEXA [4, 5], a significant part of research on that topic finds this relationship [i.a. 6–9]. Studies showing a correlation between the indices and BMD values emphasize the great diagnostic importance of this method, as patients could be early diagnosed during a routine visit to the dentist [10–12]. This review aims to evaluate the accuracy of various mandibular radiomorphometric indices in comparison with DEXA BMD measurements in the diagnosis of osteopenia and osteoporosis based on a meta-analysis of the sensitivity and specificity of the indices. Materials and methods Focused question The following question was applied: Are qualitative and quantitative mandibular radiomorphometric indices reliable tools for the diagnosis of osteopenia/osteoporosis in men and women? Protocol The present systematic review has been prepared following the guidelines of Preferred Report Items Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) [13]. Study selection The materials for analysis were collected in August 2023 by searching three databases: PubMed Central® (United States National Institutes of Health’s National Library of Medicine), Web of Science® (Institute of Scientific Information – Clarivate Analytics), and Scopus® (Elsevier). No restriction on the year of publication was imposed during the search, but a filter was applied towards only English-language articles. The following keywords were used in each database: radiomorphometric indices AND mandible OR orthopantomography OR orthopantomograms AND bone mineral density. The selection consisted of three stages – screening by the title, abstract and full text. The review was performed independently by two researchers (J.H. and A.S.), and the final results and any discrepancies regarding the inclusion or exclusion of particular publications were then discussed. fetched_contents.text: Association Between Mandibular Cortical Erosion and Bone Mineral Density Assessed by Phalangeal Ultrasound and Dual Energy X-Ray Absorptiometry in Spanish Women Abstract Background and Objectives: Analysing the characteristics of the mandibular bone through panoramic radiographs could be useful as a prescreening tool for detecting individuals with osteoporosis. The aims of this study were to evaluate the possible associations between the mandibular cortical index (MCI) and bone mineral density (BMD) in various bone regions, to investigate whether BMD better identifies moderate–severe mandibular erosion or severe mandibular erosion, and to establish BMD cut-off points to identify individuals with moderate or severe mandibular cortical erosion. Methods: This study analysed 179 Spanish Caucasian women between September 2021 and June 2024. Bone measurements, including amplitude-dependent speed of sound (Ad-SOS), the ultrasound bone profiler index (UBPI), and the bone transmission time (BTT), were obtained via dual energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) for the femoral neck, lumbar spine, and trochanter and quantitative bone ultrasound (QUS) for the phalanx. The MCI was calculated via the Klemetti index from panoramic radiographs. Results: According to the Klemetti index classification, lower QUS measurements in the phalanx and DXA measurements in the femoral neck, trochanter, and lumbar spine were found in women with poorer mandibular cortical bone quality. Our results revealed that, compared with moderate cortical erosion, all the BMD measures had better AUCs when identifying severe cortical erosion. Moreover, femoral neck BMD had the largest area under the curve (AUC = 0.719) for detecting severe mandibular cortical erosion, suggesting a cut-off of <0.703 gr/cm2. Finally, predictor analysis of osteoporosis revealed that moderate and severe mandibular cortical erosion, compared with an uninjured mandibular cortical area, was independently associated with a diagnosis of osteoporosis. Conclusions: In conclusion, MCI was associated with BMD measurements assessed by QUS and DXA in various bone regions. Our results suggest that the Klemetti index could be used as a predictor of osteoporosis and fracture risk. Keywords: osteoporosis, mandibular cortical erosion, bone mineral density, panoramic radiography, Klemetti index 1. Introduction Osteoporosis is a common disease characterized by a decrease in bone density and the breakdown of bone structure, which predominantly affects postmenopausal women, but also affects older men [1]. It is considered a skeletal disorder marked by reduced bone strength, which makes bones more susceptible to fractures [1,2]. Currently, osteoporosis is diagnosed through dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA), which measures the bone mineral density (BMD) for the femoral neck, total hip, lumbar spine, and/or the 1/3 radius [3,4]. The results are expressed as a T score using appropriate reference data according to age, sex, and ethnicity. However, DXA is not available worldwide, and its cost limits its use in many countries [5]. This limitation has prompted numerous researchers to look for more affordable and accessible alternatives to DXA, such as ultrasound (QUS), peripheral DXA or quantitative computer tomography (QCT), to diagnose osteoporosis or predict the risk of future fractures [6,7,8,9]. Studies have confirmed a possible association between skeletal bone mass and mandibular bone mass [10]. Panoramic radiographs are low-cost procedures utilized as diagnostics before dental treatment, and they have potential applications beyond the dental field. Studies on MCI accuracy and diagnostic value consistently frame it as a **screening tool** rather than a diagnostic one, with relatively modest performance for osteoporosis and stronger utility for detecting low bone mineral density (BMD) or osteopenia.

For **osteoporosis**, the most directly reported sensitivity and specificity are **0.35 sensitivity (95% CI, 0.30–0.40)** and **0.88 specificity (95% CI, 0.86–0.90)** in a meta-analysis of panoramic radiography studies [N1-F1]. For **low BMD or osteopenia**, the same meta-analysis reports **0.81 sensitivity (95% CI, 0.78–0.84)** and **0.48 specificity (95% CI, 0.45–0.50)** for MCI [N1-F1]. A separate systematic review/meta-analysis of mandibular radiomorphometric indices reports that MCI can be useful as a screening tool for low BMD but should not be used as a diagnostic method [N1-F2]. It also notes that **MCW ≤ 3 mm** had the best pooled results for detecting reduced BMD, with estimated sensitivity and specificity of **0.712 (95% CI, 0.477–0.870)** and **0.804 (95% CI, 0.589–0.921)**, respectively [N1-F2].

Study populations and comparator tests are generally female-centered and compared with **DXA**. The panoramic radiography meta-analysis included **5266 females** and used **DXA** or **quantitative CT** as the reference standard [N1-F1]. The mandible radiomorphometric meta-analysis included **64 articles** and used **DEXA BMD measurements** as the reference standard [N1-F2]. In the broader context, studies often compare MCI with **DXA, quantitative CT, or QUS** and emphasize that radiomorphometric indices are not recommended as a replacement for DXA [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The review also notes that some studies suggest no clear relationship between radiomorphometric indices and BMD, while others find a significant relationship [N1-F2].

The evidence supports **validation against gold standards**. The panoramic radiography meta-analysis explicitly uses DXA or quantitative CT as the reference standard [N1-F1], and the mandible radiomorphometric meta-analysis uses DEXA BMD measurements [N1-F2]. The evidence base is therefore anchored in comparison to the accepted gold standard for BMD, but the reported accuracy is generally lower for osteoporosis than for osteopenia [N1-F1][N1-F2].

Overall, the studies suggest that MCI has **moderate diagnostic value for screening low BMD**, especially osteopenia, but only **weak diagnostic value for osteoporosis** [N1-F1][N1-F2].

## Integrated final answer: MCI accuracy and diagnostic value for markedly eroded mandibular cortex

The evidence base on the Mandibular Cortical Index (MCI) is clear in one important respect: **MCI is best understood as a screening tool, not a diagnostic one**. Across the branch reports, MCI is repeatedly described as useful for identifying patients with low bone mineral density (BMD) or osteopenia, but the same sources caution that it should not be used as a diagnostic method [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This distinction is especially important when assessing **markedly eroded mandibular cortex**, because erosion can distort both appearance and interpretation while leaving the MCI still useful only at the level of prescreening.

### 1) Overall accuracy and diagnostic value

The branch reports indicate that MCI has **moderate sensitivity for detecting low BMD or osteopenia**, but **relatively weak sensitivity for osteoporosis**. In one meta-analysis of panoramic radiography studies, MCI showed **0.35 sensitivity (95% CI, 0.30–0.40)** for osteoporosis and **0.81 sensitivity (95% CI, 0.78–0.84)** for osteopenia [N1-F1]. For osteoporosis, the specificity was **0.88 (95% CI, 0.86–0.90)**, while for osteopenia it was **0.48 (95% CI, 0.45–0.50)** [N1-F1]. A separate systematic review/meta-analysis of mandibular radiomorphometric indices reported that **MCW ≤ 3 mm** had the best pooled results for detecting reduced BMD, with sensitivity 0.712 (95% CI, 0.477–0.870) and specificity 0.804 (95% CI, 0.589–0.921) [N1-F2].

The key takeaway is that MCI is **not a high-specificity test for osteoporosis**. Its high sensitivity for osteopenia makes it useful as an **early-screening tool**, but its lower specificity for osteoporosis means it can miss true disease or generate many false positives if used as a standalone diagnostic test [N1-F1][N1-F2]. The branch reports therefore support a cautious interpretation: MCI is **useful for flagging risk, not for confirming or ruling out osteoporosis** [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### 2) Study populations, comparator tests, and gold-standard validation

The evidence is largely based on female populations and compared with **DXA** or **quantitative CT** as the gold standard. The panoramic radiography meta-analysis included **5266 females** and used DXA or quantitative CT as the reference standard [N1-F1]. The mandible radiomorphometric meta-analysis included **64 articles** and used **DEXA BMD measurements** as the reference standard [N1-F2]. The erosion-specific study in Spanish women also used **DXA and QUS** measurements to assess BMD and correlated MCI with those values [N2-F3].

This means the reported accuracy figures are **validated against established BMD standards**, but they are still limited by the inherent imprecision of radiomorphometric indices. The branch reports emphasize that radiomorphometric indices are **not recommended as a replacement for DXA** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. In other words, the studies show MCI can be useful in screening, but they do not support using it as a substitute for DXA in diagnostic decision-making.

### 3) How markedly eroded mandible affects MCI interpretation

Markedly eroded mandible changes both the **appearance** and **measurement** of MCI. The MCI is a **qualitative index** that assesses the **appearance of the mandibular endosteum** and classifies the mandibular cortex [N4-R2]. In the erosion-specific study, panoramic radiographs were described as useful as a **prescreening tool for osteoporosis**, and the authors noted that in individuals with osteoporosis, the mandibular cortical bone undergoes resorption that can be observed on panoramic radiographs [N2-F3]. This implies that erosion is a visible sign of underlying bone loss rather than a random feature.

The evidence suggests that erosion can make MCI interpretation less reliable. Because the MCI is qualitative and subject to **examiner subjectivism**, it is especially vulnerable to variation in measurement and classification [N1-F2][N4-R2]. The erosion study also reports that **age, sex, and mandibular morphometric parameters** significantly influence MCW and cortical erosion, indicating that anatomical variability can affect the index [N6-R5]. That means erosion does not just change the image; it can change the **measurement framework** and the **classification of the cortex**.

### 4) Does erosion lead to false-negative or false-positive results?

The evidence does not directly report a single, universal false-negative or false-positive rate for markedly eroded mandibles, but it provides enough direction to infer likely effects. Because the MCI is a qualitative measure, erosion can distort the visual appearance of the cortex and thus affect measurement consistency [N4-R2]. The erosion-specific study also found that **BMD measures had better AUCs for identifying severe cortical erosion than moderate erosion**, suggesting that erosion may improve detection of true low BMD in some contexts [N2-F3].

At the same time, because the MCI is prone to **operator dependence**, it is plausible that erosion could lead to **false positives** if erosion is mistaken for normal cortex, or **false negatives** if erosion is overlooked or misclassified [N1-F2][N4-R2]. The branch reports therefore support the conclusion that **eroded mandibles may increase diagnostic uncertainty**, not reduce it.

### 5) Erosion-specific diagnostic value and threshold evidence

The erosion-specific evidence indicates that **erosion is associated with lower BMD**, which in turn affects MCI interpretation. In the Spanish women study, women with poorer mandibular cortical bone quality had lower QUS and DXA measurements, and MCI was associated with BMD assessed by QUS and DXA in various bone regions [N2-F3]. The same study found that **BMD measures had better AUCs for identifying severe cortical erosion than moderate erosion**, which supports the idea that erosion severity is linked to lower BMD and thus to lower MCI values in some contexts [N2-F3].

On sensitivity and specificity, the evidence is mixed but consistent in direction. For severe cortical erosion, the study reports that **femoral neck BMD had the largest AUC** for detection, with a cut-off of <0.703 g/cm² [N2-F3]. This implies that erosion may improve the ability to detect true low BMD, but it does not necessarily improve overall specificity. The study also reports that **moderate and severe mandibular cortical erosion were independently associated with osteoporosis diagnosis** [N2-F3], suggesting erosion can increase sensitivity for osteoporosis, but the evidence does not show that it improves specificity enough to make MCI diagnostic.

The threshold evidence is strongest for **severe erosion**, where **BMD cut-off points** were established for identifying individuals with moderate or severe cortical erosion [N2-F3]. The erosion-related evidence set also discusses **AUCs and optimal cut-off values of bone density** for identifying moderate or severe cortical erosion, which directly supports the need for erosion-aware thresholds [N6-R3]. Taken together, the branch reports suggest that **erosion-aware classification rules and BMD thresholds are needed**, rather than a single universal MCI cutoff [N2-F3][N6-R3].

### 6) Practical and clinical implications

Clinically, MCI is most useful in **screening settings** and in **dental or low-resource contexts** where rapid, accessible assessment of BMD risk is needed [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-R1]. It is also described as a **very simple and practical method** that can be effectively assessed on panoramic radiographs [N5-R1]. This makes it most useful in routine dental practice, postmenopausal screening, and settings where DXA is not available or too costly [N4-R1][N4-R4][N5-R2].

MCI is least useful in **diagnostic settings** or where high specificity is required. The systematic reviews explicitly state that radiomorphometric indices, including MCI, are useful as a **screening tool but not as a diagnostic method** [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This means MCI is less suitable for confirming a diagnosis, ruling out osteoporosis, or guiding treatment decisions. It is also less useful when the clinical need is to distinguish between mild and severe osteoporosis, because the evidence base suggests that MCI has only modest sensitivity and specificity for osteoporosis [N1-F1][N1-F2].

The main limitations are **operator dependence, reproducibility, and anatomical variability**. The systematic review notes that MCI is prone to **examiner subjectivism** and that the general methodological quality of retrieved studies was low [N1-F2]. The same source also states that radiomorphometric indices are useful as a screening tool but should not be used as a diagnostic method [N1-F2]. Another source explicitly describes the MCI as a **qualitative index** that assesses the appearance of the mandibular endosteum [N4-R2], which reinforces the idea that interpretation can vary by observer. The erosion-specific study further indicates that **age, sex, and mandibular morphometric parameters** significantly influence MCW and cortical erosion, suggesting that anatomical variability can affect the measurement and interpretation of the index [N6-R5].

### 7) What clinicians should expect in terms of diagnostic certainty

Clinicians should expect **moderate diagnostic certainty at best**. The evidence supports a screening role rather than a diagnostic role, and the reported sensitivity/specificity for osteoporosis is relatively low [N1-F1][N1-F2]. For osteopenia, the sensitivity is much higher, but specificity is still limited [N1-F1]. This means that MCI is best used to **flag possible risk**, not to substitute for DXA or another gold-standard test.

In the context of **markedly eroded mandible**, clinicians should expect that erosion can distort appearance and measurement, and that the MCI may become less reliable. Because the MCI is qualitative and subject to observer variability, erosion can plausibly lead to **false positives** if erosion is mistaken for normal cortex, or **false negatives** if erosion is overlooked or misclassified [N4-R2][N1-F2]. Therefore, clinicians should interpret MCI findings cautiously and use MCI only as one part of a broader assessment [N4-R2][N1-F2].

### 8) Bottom line
